QuestionIdentifierType is the module identifier alias.
    • Concept introduced: the id-plus-request command shape, and validation by delegation. Where the create path lets the request itself be the command (see ConferenceCategoryCreateRequest), the update path cannot: the id comes from the route, not the body, so a wrapper is needed. Implementing ICommandWithRequest<out TRequest> is what makes that wrapper cheap. The interface contributes one member, TRequest Request, and in exchange the framework registers a CommandRequestValidator<TCommand, TRequest> that delegates to the existing IValidator<TRequest> via FluentValidation's SetValidator (MMCA.Common/Source/Core/MMCA.Common.Application/UseCases/ICommandWithRequest.cs:5-11). So QuestionUpdateRequestValidator is written against the request, and the command inherits it for free with no UpdateQuestionCommandValidator file to keep in sync. Registration uses TryAdd semantics, so an explicit IValidator<TCommand> still wins when a command needs a rule spanning the id and the body. The second marker, ICacheInvalidating, opts the command into the caching decorator so a successful update evicts the question read cache. [Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven] assesses whether writes are explicit intents flowing through a uniform pipeline: this record is pure intent, and both cross-cutting behaviors attach declaratively through marker interfaces (ADR-014).
    • Walkthrough: sealed record UpdateQuestionCommand(QuestionIdentifierType Id, QuestionUpdateRequest Request) implementing both markers (:9); CachePrefix (:12) returns "{typeof(Question).FullName}:", the key namespace the caching decorator wipes on success. The positional Request parameter satisfies the interface's Request property with no extra code.
    • Where it's used: constructed by QuestionsController from the route id and body (QuestionsController.cs:109) and handled by UpdateQuestionHandler.

The doc comment on the parameter (:9-12) states the rule precisely: it is "bound at the API edge, never from the request body", and when it is false the handler "ignores the organizer-only request field IsTopSpeaker and keeps the entity's current value".     • What it is: the handler for UpdateQuestionCommand. It loads the Question, stamps the concurrency token, enforces BR-137 (question type and target entity are immutable once any answer exists), delegates the mutation to the aggregate, saves, and returns the updated DTO.
    • Depends on: ICommandHandler<in TCommand, TResult> (UpdateQuestionHandler.cs:9,22), IUnitOfWork (:8,20), QuestionDTOMapper (:2,21), Result and Error (:10), the Question aggregate plus the three answer entities EventQuestionAnswer (:3,42), SessionQuestionAnswer (:5,49), and SpeakerQuestionAnswer (:6,59), and ILogger<T> (:1,22).
    • Concept introduced: the conditional cross-aggregate guard, and short-circuit existence checks. Two mechanisms are worth studying here. The first is optimistic concurrency: repository.SetOriginalRowVersion(entity, command.Request.RowVersion) (:36) stamps the client's last-seen token onto the tracked entity so that, as the source comment says (:34-35), a concurrent edit surfaces as a DbUpdateConcurrencyException mapped to 409 instead of silent last-write-wins. Every update handler in this group opens with the same three lines. The second is the BR-137 guard (:38-73), and its shape is the lesson: the expensive part runs only if it can matter. The whole block is inside if (entity.QuestionType != command.Request.QuestionType || entity.QuestionEntity != command.Request.QuestionEntity) (:39-40), so an edit that leaves both fields alone issues zero extra queries. Inside, three ExistsAsync probes run against the answer tables in sequence, each guarded by if (!hasAnswers) (:47, :55), so the second and third queries are skipped as soon as any answer is found. ExistsAsync on a read repository compiles to an existence check rather than materializing rows. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] assesses whether the data access does the minimum work required: the guard is both branch-skipped and short-circuited. [Rubric §4, Domain-Driven Design]: the rule lives in the handler rather than the aggregate because it spans three other aggregates that the Question cannot see. [Rubric §8, Data Architecture]: the concurrency token is the row-level conflict-detection mechanism.
    • Walkthrough: HandleAsync (:25) gets the typed repository (:29) and loads by id (:30), returning Error.NotFound tagged with source and target when absent (:31-32). It stamps the row version (:36). The BR-137 block (:38-73) probes event answers (:42-45), then session answers if still clean (:49-53), then speaker answers (:59-63), each with the predicate a => a.QuestionId.Equals(entity.Id); the source comment at :57-58 records why speaker answers count too, namely that a question already answered on a speaker profile must stay type-stable. When any answer exists it returns Error.Validation with the stable code "Question.ImmutableAfterAnswers" (:67-72). Otherwise it calls entity.Update(QuestionText, QuestionEntity, QuestionType, Sort, IsRequired) (:75-80) and propagates the aggregate's errors on failure (:82-83). On success it saves (:85), emits LogQuestionUpdated (:87), and returns Result.Success(dtoMapper.MapToDTO(entity)) (:89). The [LoggerMessage] (:92-93) declares the template "Question {QuestionId} updated".
    • Why it's built this way: note the three probes use GetReadRepository (:42, :49, :59) while the entity itself came from GetRepository (:29). The read repository is the no-tracking path: these answers are only being counted, never modified, so tracking them would be wasted work and would enlarge the change set that SaveChangesAsync inspects. The handler opens no transaction and evicts no cache itself: the transactional and caching decorators do that, driven by the command's markers (ADR-014).
    • Where it's used: injected into QuestionsController as ICommandHandler<UpdateQuestionCommand, Result<QuestionDTO>> (QuestionsController.cs:34) and invoked on PUT (:109).

    • What it is: the most guarded update handler in the module. It loads the Session, stamps the concurrency token, rejects an attempt to move the session between events (BR-140), loads the parent Event to validate the room assignment and double-booking (BR-130), delegates to the aggregate, computes the BR-86 date-range advisory, saves, and returns an UpdateSessionResult.

    • Concept introduced: four distinct guard styles in one method, each chosen to fit the rule. This handler is worth reading line by line because it demonstrates the codebase's whole vocabulary of write-time checks:
      1. The immutability guard (:37-44). command.Request.EventId != entity.EventId returns Error.UnprocessableEntity with the stable code "Session.EventId.Immutable" and the message "Session cannot be moved between events." The handler owns this rule, not the aggregate, because only the handler sees both the submitted value and the stored one. UnprocessableEntity rather than Validation is the right classification: the payload is well-formed, the requested state transition is not allowed.
      2. The delegated cross-aggregate check (:57-65). Room ownership and slot overlap are pushed into the shared static SessionRoomScheduling.ValidateRoomAssignmentAsync, which the create path calls too, with excludeSessionId: command.Id (:63) so a session does not collide with itself. Errors propagate unchanged (:66-67).
      3. The domain guard (:69-86). Everything expressible from the session's own state goes to entity.Update(...), whose Result failure is propagated as-is.
      4. The advisory (:89-91). BR-86 does not block anything: IsOutsideEventDateRange returns a bool that rides out on UpdateSessionResult and becomes an X-Warning header. Also note the read strategy on the parent event (:48-52): GetByIdAsync(entity.EventId, includes: [nameof(Event.Rooms)], asTracking: false, ...). The rooms are eager-loaded because the room validation needs them in memory, and tracking is off because the event is read-only in this flow, so it must not join the change set. [Rubric §4, Domain-Driven Design] assesses where rules live: state-local rules are in the aggregate, cross-aggregate rules are in the handler or a shared validator. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability]: one targeted include, no tracking, one extra aggregate read. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]: stable error codes and a non-fatal warning channel.
    • Walkthrough: HandleAsync (:23) gets the session repository (:27), loads by id (:28), and returns Error.NotFound when absent (:29-30). It stamps the row version (:34). The BR-140 check runs next (:37-44), before any further I/O, so an illegal move costs one query. It then loads the parent event with rooms, untracked (:47-52), returning Error.NotFound targeted at Event when the parent is missing (:53-54). Room validation follows (:57-65), passing the repository, the parent event, the requested RoomId, StartsAt, EndsAt, the self-exclusion id, and the handler name as the error source. entity.Update(...) receives the fourteen mutable fields (:69-83) and its failure is propagated (:85-86). hasDateRangeWarning is computed before the save (:89-91) from the requested times and the event's StartDate / EndDate. Then SaveChangesAsync with ConfigureAwait(false) (:93), LogSessionUpdated (:95), and Result.Success(new UpdateSessionResult(dtoMapper.MapToDTO(entity), hasDateRangeWarning)) (:97). The private static IsOutsideEventDateRange (:104-113) converts each nullable DateTime with DateOnly.FromDateTime and returns true when the start falls before the event's first day (:108-109) or the end falls after its last day (:110-111), otherwise false (:112).
    • Why it's built this way: the guard order is deliberate cost ordering. The cheapest rejections (not found, immutable event) come first, the extra database read for the parent event happens only once those pass, and the aggregate's own validation runs last. The comparison uses DateOnly rather than the raw DateTime because an event's dates are calendar days (DateOnly), so comparing a timestamp against them without truncation would report a session starting on the morning of day one as out of range.
    • Where it's used: injected into SessionsController as ICommandHandler<UpdateSessionCommand, Result<UpdateSessionResult>> (SessionsController.cs:45) and invoked on PUT (:306-308); the controller appends the X-Warning header when the flag is set (:314-317), then returns result.Value.Session (:320).

    MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application.Categories.UseCases.AddCategoryItem · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application/Categories/UseCases/AddCategoryItem/AddCategoryItemCommand.cs:14 · Level 7 · record

    • What it is: the write intent for adding one child item to an existing conference Category aggregate. It carries the owning category id, an optional item id, the display name, and the sort order.
    • Depends on: ICacheInvalidating from MMCA.Common.Application.UseCases (AddCategoryItemCommand.cs:2,18) and the Category domain type, referenced only to build the cache key prefix (:1,21). ConferenceCategoryIdentifierType and CategoryItemIdentifierType are the module identifier aliases, both int (MMCA.ADC.Conference.Shared/MMCA.ADC.Conference.GlobalUsings.IdentifierType.cs:5-6; see primer).
    • Concept introduced: the child-add command shape. A positional record is the whole request: it holds no behavior, and the aggregate decides what the add means. Two details carry weight. First, CategoryItemId is nullable (CategoryItemIdentifierType?, :16), and the XML doc says why (:11): the Sessionize import supplies the source-assigned id, while a manual add leaves it null for database-generated identity. The domain honors both branches, because CategoryItem is marked [IdValueGenerated] yet still keeps a supplied id when one is given (MMCA.ADC.Conference.Domain/Categories/CategoryItem.cs:13,61). Second, implementing ICacheInvalidating opts the command into the caching decorator of the CQRS pipeline, so a successful add evicts the category read cache without the handler touching a cache API. [Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven] assesses whether writes are explicit intents flowing through one uniform pipeline: this record is the intent, and the marker interface is how a cross-cutting concern attaches to it declaratively. [Rubric §10, Cross-Cutting]: cache eviction is declared on the contract and applied centrally, never hand-rolled per handler.
    • Walkthrough: the positional parameters are CategoryId (:15), the nullable CategoryItemId (:16), Name (:17), and Sort (:18); the record is sealed and implements ICacheInvalidating (:14,18). The single member, CachePrefix (:21), returns $"{typeof(Category).FullName}:", the key namespace the caching decorator wipes on success. Keying off typeof(Category) rather than typeof(CategoryItem) is deliberate: items are read as part of their parent, so the parent's cached reads are the stale ones.
    • Why it's built this way: a positional record gives value equality and immutability for free, and deriving the prefix from the entity's FullName keeps producer (this command) and consumer (the query cache) agreed on one string with no shared constant to drift.
    • Where it's used: constructed by CategoryItemsController on POST (MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/CategoryItemsController.cs:126-130), validated by AddCategoryItemCommandValidator, and handled by AddCategoryItemHandler.

    • What it is: the Mapperly-generated mapper that turns a CategoryItem domain entity into its wire-facing CategoryItemDTO.
    • Depends on: IEntityDTOMapper<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType> from MMCA.Common.Application.Interfaces (CategoryItemDTOMapper.cs:3,13), CategoryItem and CategoryItemDTO (:1-2), and the Mapperly source generator (Riok.Mapperly.Abstractions, :4).
    • Concept introduced: source-generated DTO mapping (ADR-001). The class is sealed partial and carries [Mapper] (:11-12); Mapperly writes the body of the partial CategoryItemDTO MapToDTO(...) declaration (:16) at compile time by name-matching properties, so there is no runtime reflection, no expression tree, and no hand-written field copy to fall behind the entity. This is the split ADR-001 describes: property-name-parallel entity/DTO pairs get generated mappers, and only genuine mismatches need hand-written code. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses whether the domain model is shielded from the wire contract: the entity and the DTO stay two separate shapes, so a domain rename cannot silently change the API payload (it breaks the build instead). [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability]: compile-time mapping costs no reflection at runtime.
    • Walkthrough: MapToDTO (:16) is the generated single-entity conversion. MapToDTOs (:19) is hand-written because the interface asks for a collection overload: it null-guards with ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(entityCollection) (:21), then projects each element through MapToDTO into a materialized array with the collection expression [.. entityCollection.Select(MapToDTO)] (:22). Materializing rather than returning a lazy sequence matters, because the caller may dispose the DbContext before enumeration.
    • Why it's built this way: implementing the framework's IEntityDTOMapper contract is what lets the mapper be discovered by assembly scanning and injected, so no caller ever news it or hardcodes a conversion.
    • Where it's used: composed as the child mapper inside ConferenceCategoryDTOMapper and injected into AddCategoryItemHandler to shape the newly added item for the response.

    • Concept introduced: the request-is-the-command idiom. Rather than a command record wrapping a request record, the create path lets one record class be both the bound wire contract and the handler input. Implementing ICreateRequest is what lets the generic entity-request-mapper machinery recognize it (the type's own <remarks> says exactly that, :8-9), and ICacheInvalidating opts it into cache eviction on success. Contrast the update path, which does wrap a request in a command (UpdateConferenceCategoryCommand) because an update needs the route id and the concurrency token alongside the body. [Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven]: writes are explicit intents, and marker interfaces are how cross-cutting behavior attaches to them declaratively. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design]: the create shape is a first-class named type with compiler-enforced required fields, not an anonymous bag.
    • Walkthrough: CachePrefix (:13) returns the same Category full-name prefix the item commands use. Id (:16) is init-only and optional (the doc comment at :15 calls it auto-generated when not provided). Title (:19) is required string, the one field the create validator guards. Sort (:22) is an int display order defaulting to zero. Type (:25) is an optional discriminator string, documented as "session" or "speaker" (:24).

    • Where it's used: bound from the body by ConferenceCategoriesController (MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/ConferenceCategoriesController.cs:94), validated by ConferenceCategoryCreateRequestValidator, translated by ConferenceCategoryCreateRequestMapper, and handled by CreateConferenceCategoryHandler.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: because Id is a non-nullable int, an omitted id binds as 0 and reaches Category.Create as 0, not null, so the id ?? ... fallback at MMCA.ADC.Conference.Domain/Categories/Category.cs:69 is not what supplies the key on this path. Category is annotated [IdValueGenerated] (Category.cs:15), so a zero id is the unset sentinel the persistence layer replaces on insert.

Instead of repeating RuleFor(x => x.Text).NotEmpty().MaximumLength(...) inside every validator that carries question text, the constraints live once in a small AbstractValidator<T> subclass whose constructor takes a property selector. A concrete validator folds it in with FluentValidation's Include(...). Because the rule set is generic in T and receives the selector, the same type validates a create request or an update request, each pointing the selector at its own property. This is the hand-rolled cousin of the framework's RequiredStringRules<T>; the difference is that this one also pins the error codes. [Rubric §24, Forms/Validation/UX Safety] assesses whether input constraints are declared once and applied consistently: centralizing the question-text contract here keeps every entry path in agreement. [Rubric §1, SOLID]: one rule set, one responsibility, reused rather than copied.
    • Walkthrough: the class is sealed and generic in T (:12). The expression-bodied constructor (:15) binds RuleFor(selector) and chains two clauses: NotEmpty() with the message "You must enter a Question Text" and error code Question.QuestionText.Required (:17), then MaximumLength(QuestionInvariants.QuestionTextMaxLength) (1000 characters, MMCA.ADC.Conference.Domain/Questions/QuestionInvariants.cs:13) with a length message and error code Question.QuestionText.MaxLength (:18). The stable WithErrorCode(...) strings are what the API error-mapping layer keys on, so they are part of the contract, not decoration.
    • Why it's built this way: sourcing the bound from QuestionInvariants rather than a literal keeps the application-layer validator and the domain guard (QuestionInvariants.cs:59) citing one constant, so a limit change cannot drift between layers.

    • Concept introduced: rule-set composition via Include. Rather than restating the item-field rules inline, the constructor folds two reusable, selector-parameterized rule objects into this validator: Include(new CategoryItemNameRules<AddCategoryItemCommand>(p => p.Name)) (:11) and Include(new CategoryItemSortRules<AddCategoryItemCommand>(p => p.Sort)) (:12). Each rule set is the same device QuestionTextRules<T> teaches, applied to category items: the name rule enforces non-empty plus a 500-character bound sourced from CategoryInvariants.CategoryItemNameMaxLength (MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application/Categories/Validation/ConferenceCategoryValidationRules.cs:30-33, constant at MMCA.ADC.Conference.Domain/Categories/CategoryInvariants.cs:17), and the sort rule enforces GreaterThanOrEqualTo(0) (ConferenceCategoryValidationRules.cs:43-45).     • What it is: the handler for AddCategoryItemCommand: load the owning Category, delegate the add to the root, persist, log, and return the new item's DTO.
    • Depends on: ICommandHandler<in TCommand, TResult> (AddCategoryItemHandler.cs:6,18), IUnitOfWork (:5,16), CategoryItemDTOMapper (:2,17), Result and Error (:7), and ILogger<AddCategoryItemHandler> (:1,18).
    • Concept introduced: routing a child mutation through the aggregate root. The handler never inserts a CategoryItem row; it loads the Category and calls category.AddCategoryItem(...) (:30), so the aggregate enforces its own consistency (the DDD boundary rule from Group 02). What lives behind that one call is substantial: the case-insensitive name-uniqueness rule BR-138, the CategoryItem factory, and a CategoryItemChanged domain event (MMCA.ADC.Conference.Domain/Categories/Category.cs:131-153). The handler is correspondingly thin, because validation, caching, and the transaction are applied by the decorator pipeline around it (see primer and Group 05). [Rubric §4, Domain-Driven Design]: mutations go through the root. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability]: the [LoggerMessage] source-generated log (:41-42) is compile-time and allocation-free, no boxing and no runtime format parsing.

A null category returns Error.NotFound tagged with source and target for diagnostics (:27-28). It then calls category.AddCategoryItem(command.CategoryItemId, command.Name, command.Sort) (:30) and short-circuits with the aggregate's own errors on failure (:31-32). On success it awaits SaveChangesAsync with ConfigureAwait(false) (:34), emits LogCategoryItemAdded (:36), and returns Result.Success(dtoMapper.MapToDTO(result.Value!)) (:38), mapping the very item the aggregate just created rather than re-reading it.
    • Why it's built this way: the handler opens no transaction and evicts no cache itself; the transactional and caching decorators do that, driven by the marker interface on AddCategoryItemCommand. That keeps the handler focused and the cross-cutting behavior uniform across every command in the module.
    • Where it's used: injected into CategoryItemsController as ICommandHandler<AddCategoryItemCommand, Result<CategoryItemDTO>> (MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/CategoryItemsController.cs:63) and invoked on POST.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: AddCategoryItem returns the created entity, so the DTO is mapped from the in-memory instance. Any value the database assigns during SaveChangesAsync is reflected only because EF writes the generated key back onto that tracked instance; nothing in this handler re-queries.

The domain Result is returned unchanged (:57), so an aggregate-level failure (an unknown item id, for instance) reaches the caller with its own error intact.

Both infrastructure awaits carry ConfigureAwait(false) (:34-35), the library-code convention (ADR-049); the mapper await at :27 does not, because it does no I/O.     AddEventQuestionAnswerCommand

    MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application.Events.UseCases.AddEventQuestionAnswer · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application/Events/UseCases/AddEventQuestionAnswer/AddEventQuestionAnswerCommand.cs:11 · Level 8 · record (sealed)

    • What it is: the write intent for recording an answer to a conference question against an Event: which event, which question, the answer text, and optionally an explicit id for the new answer row.
    • Depends on: ICacheInvalidating from MMCA.Common.Application.UseCases (AddEventQuestionAnswerCommand.cs:2,15), the Event domain type used only to build the cache prefix (AddEventQuestionAnswerCommand.cs:1,18), and the module identifier aliases EventIdentifierType, EventQuestionAnswerIdentifierType, and QuestionIdentifierType (see the primer).
    • Concept introduced, the cache-invalidating child-add command. A mutation opts into cache eviction by implementing ICacheInvalidating and exposing a CachePrefix; the caching decorator in the CQRS pipeline (Group 05) purges every cached read under that prefix once the command succeeds. Two details generalize to every add-child command in this unit. First, the prefix is keyed on the aggregate root (typeof(Event).FullName, AddEventQuestionAnswerCommand.cs:18), not on the child type, because a cached event read carries its answers with it. Second, the child id is nullable (EventQuestionAnswerIdentifierType?, AddEventQuestionAnswerCommand.cs:13): a Sessionize import can supply the source-assigned id, while an interactive add leaves it null. [Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven] assesses whether writes are explicit intents flowing through one pipeline: the record is the intent and the marker interface is how the cross-cutting cache concern attaches declaratively, so no handler touches the cache. [Rubric §10, Cross-Cutting]: caching is a pipeline concern, not hand-rolled per use case.
    • Walkthrough: a sealed record with four positional parameters, EventId, the nullable EventQuestionAnswerId, QuestionId, and the string AnswerValue (AddEventQuestionAnswerCommand.cs:11-15), plus the single computed CachePrefix => $"{typeof(Event).FullName}:" (AddEventQuestionAnswerCommand.cs:18). There is no behavior here; the upsert rule, the published-event check, and the question-type check all live in AddEventQuestionAnswerHandler.
    • Why it's built this way: a positional record gives immutability and value equality for free, and keeping the payload to plain identifiers plus the answer text means the caller cannot smuggle in an owner id: the handler derives the answering user from ICurrentUserService instead.
    • Where it's used: constructed by the answers controller with a null child id (MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/EventQuestionAnswersController.cs:159), validated by AddEventQuestionAnswerCommandValidator, and handled by AddEventQuestionAnswerHandler.

    PublishedEventSpecification

    MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application.Events.Specifications · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application/Events/Specifications/PublishedEventSpecification.cs:11 · Level 8 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: a one-line query filter object that restricts an event query to published events only. It is how BR-108 ("non-privileged readers see only published events") is expressed as data rather than as an if inside every read endpoint.
    • Depends on: Specification<TEntity, TIdentifierType> from MMCA.Common.Domain.Specifications (PublishedEventSpecification.cs:3,11), the Event aggregate and its EventIdentifierType alias (PublishedEventSpecification.cs:2,11), and System.Linq.Expressions (PublishedEventSpecification.cs:1,14).
    • Concept introduced, authorization expressed as a specification. The specification pattern itself is taught in Group 03; what this type introduces is using it as a security filter. The base class exposes a Criteria expression that the repository composes into the EF query, so the restriction is applied in SQL rather than after materialization: an unpublished event is never loaded, never counted in a page total, and never reaches the serializer. Because the filter is a first-class object, the decision "does this caller get the filter" becomes a nullable value at the call site instead of branching query code. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether authorization is enforced at the data boundary rather than in the view: here a non-privileged reader's query cannot return an unpublished row at all. [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability]: pushing the predicate into the expression tree keeps paging counts correct and avoids over-fetching.
    • Walkthrough: the whole type is a single expression-bodied override, public override Expression<Func<Event, bool>> Criteria => e => e.IsPublished (PublishedEventSpecification.cs:14). There is no constructor and no state, so an instance is free to allocate per request.
    • Why it's built this way: keeping BR-108 in one named type means the four event read endpoints share one definition of "visible event", and the class name makes the business rule greppable. Inheriting from the framework Specification<TEntity, TIdentifierType> base lets the same object flow through the generic query service and repository without an ADC-specific overload.
    • Where it's used: EventsController builds it through the private helper GetPublishedEventSpecification(), which returns null (no filter) when currentUserService.IsPrivilegedConferenceReader() and a new instance otherwise (MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/EventsController.cs:66-67). The helper is passed as the specification: argument on four read paths (EventsController.cs:82, EventsController.cs:112, EventsController.cs:141, EventsController.cs:171).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the gate is the read audience, not the Organizer role alone. IsPrivilegedConferenceReader() also admits ContentEditor, because an editor who reads every session must also read the events those sessions belong to (EventsController.cs:60-65). The predicate here does not exclude soft-deleted rows; that is handled separately by the EF global query filter (see Group 07).

    AddEventQuestionAnswerHandler

    MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application.Events.UseCases.AddEventQuestionAnswer · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application/Events/UseCases/AddEventQuestionAnswer/AddEventQuestionAnswerHandler.cs:17 · Level 9 · class (sealed partial)

    • What it is: the handler that records a user's answer to an event question. It is the most rule-dense handler in this unit: it gates on the event being published, cross-checks the question, and then performs an upsert rather than a blind insert.
    • Depends on: IUnitOfWork (AddEventQuestionAnswerHandler.cs:18), ICurrentUserService (:19), EventQuestionAnswerDTOMapper (:20), ILogger<AddEventQuestionAnswerHandler> (:21), the ICommandHandler<in TCommand, TResult> contract (:21), the Event aggregate with its EventQuestionAnswer children, EventInvariants (:38), Question plus QuestionInvariants (:63,75), and Result/Error.
    • Concept introduced, the add that is really an upsert (BR-107). A user answering the same question twice must not accumulate rows; the second submission replaces the first. The handler encodes that as an identity lookup on the triple (current user, question, event): the event is already the aggregate being loaded, so the search reduces to scanning the loaded children for !a.IsDeleted && a.QuestionId == command.QuestionId && a.CreatedBy == userId (AddEventQuestionAnswerHandler.cs:49-50). The owner is read from ICurrentUserService (:48), never from the command, so a caller cannot answer on someone else's behalf. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether identity is derived server-side: the answering user is ambient, not a request field. [Rubric §4, DDD]: the reconciliation happens against children already loaded in the aggregate, so no second round trip and no chance of mutating an answer outside its event. [Rubric §6, CQRS]: one command, one handler, one transaction boundary at SaveChangesAsync.
    • Walkthrough: HandleAsync (AddEventQuestionAnswerHandler.cs:24-56) loads the event through unitOfWork.GetRepository<Event, EventIdentifierType>() with includes: [nameof(Event.EventQuestionAnswers)] and asTracking: true (:28-33), because the domain mutation walks that child collection and EF must be tracking it; a missing event returns Error.NotFound sourced to the handler and targeted at Event (:34-35). BR-108 is checked by delegating to EventInvariants.EnsureEventIsPublished(entity.IsPublished, ...) (:38-40), which fails with the invariant code Event.NotPublished (MMCA.ADC.Conference.Domain/Events/EventInvariants.cs:147-154). The private ValidateQuestionAsync (:58-77) then loads the Question by id and fails with the validation code Question.NotFoundOrWrongEntity when it is missing or its QuestionEntity != "Event" (BR-128, :63-72), and otherwise returns QuestionInvariants.EnsureAnswerValueMatchesQuestionType(question.QuestionType, command.AnswerValue, ...) (BR-124, :75-76), which switches on "Rating", "Text", or "Email" and rejects an unknown type outright (MMCA.ADC.Conference.Domain/Questions/QuestionInvariants.cs:115-126). Only then does the upsert branch run: an existing answer routes to UpdateExistingAnswerAsync (:52-53), which calls entity.UpdateEventQuestionAnswer(existingAnswer.Id, command.AnswerValue) and returns the mapped existing row (:79-92); otherwise CreateNewAnswerAsync calls entity.AddEventQuestionAnswer(command.EventQuestionAnswerId, command.QuestionId, command.AnswerValue) and returns the mapped new child (:94-109). Both branches persist with a single SaveChangesAsync(...).ConfigureAwait(false) and log through the source-generated LogQuestionAnswerAddedToEvent (:89-91, :106-108, :111-112).
    • Why it's built this way: the three gates run in increasing cost order, cheapest first: the aggregate is already loaded, the published flag is in memory, and only the question check costs a second query. Splitting the two upsert outcomes into private methods keeps HandleAsync readable as a decision tree while both paths share one save. The [LoggerMessage] source generator gives allocation-free structured logging ([Rubric §13, Observability & Operability]), and ConfigureAwait(false) on the infrastructure awaits follows the library convention (ADR-049).
    • Where it's used: dispatched by the answers controller through the CQRS pipeline (MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/EventQuestionAnswersController.cs:58, EventQuestionAnswersController.cs:159).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: currentUserService.UserId!.Value (AddEventQuestionAnswerHandler.cs:48) is null-forgiven, so the handler assumes an authenticated caller; the enforcement of that assumption lives in the controller's authorization attributes, not here. The success log message is identical for the update and insert branches (:111), so the log alone does not distinguish an upsert from a new answer.

Because each rule set is generic in the request type and takes a property selector, the same RoomNameRules<T> object validates a room name on this command, on UpdateRoomCommand, and on the Sessionize import path, each pointing at its own property. The alternative, restating the clauses per command, is what lets a constraint drift between the add and update endpoints. [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] assesses duplication: there is exactly one definition of each room-field constraint. [Rubric §16, Maintainability]: a constraint change is a one-file edit that propagates to every command that composed the rule.
    • Walkthrough: the constructor is six Include calls in field order, each constructing a rule set bound to the matching property: RoomNameRules on p => p.Name (AddRoomCommandValidator.cs:11), RoomSortRules on Sort (:12), RoomCapacityRules on Capacity (:13), RoomFloorRules on Floor (:14), RoomLocationRules on Location (:15), and RoomAccessibilityInfoRules on AccessibilityInfo (:16). No bespoke rule appears in this class; every constraint lives in the included types.
    • Why it's built this way: rooms are written from two directions (organizer create and Sessionize import), and shared rule sets are the mechanism that keeps both honest without a base validator class. Its update counterpart UpdateRoomCommandValidator composes the same six sets, which is the clearest demonstration that the composition is the point.
    • Where it's used: resolved and invoked by the pipeline's validation decorator (Group 05) for AddRoomCommand, before AddRoomHandler runs.

    AddRoomHandler

    MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application.Events.UseCases.AddRoom · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application/Events/UseCases/AddRoom/AddRoomHandler.cs:18 · Level 9 · class (sealed partial)

    • What it is: the handler that adds a room to an event. It carries two concerns no other handler in this unit has: it allocates the room's primary key itself from a reserved range, and it retries in a fresh DI scope when a concurrent add wins the same key.
    • Depends on: IUnitOfWork (AddRoomHandler.cs:19), IServiceScopeFactory from Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection (:1,20), RoomDTOMapper (:21), ILogger<AddRoomHandler> (:22), the ICommandHandler<in TCommand, TResult> contract (:22), the Event and Room types, EventInvariants for the reserved-range constants (:87,93,95), IReadRepository<TEntity, TIdentifierType> via GetReadRepository (:84), and Result/Error.
    • Concept introduced, reserved-range key allocation with a bounded collision retry. Room ids are application-assigned: the integer primary key is the Sessionize id, so the database identity column cannot own the value or an import would overwrite an organizer's room. The codebase resolves this by reserving a high block for manually created rooms, EventInvariants.RoomManualIdRangeStart = 999_999_000 through RoomManualIdRangeEnd = 999_999_999 (MMCA.ADC.Conference.Domain/Events/EventInvariants.cs:53,56), and having the handler pick the next free id inside it. That read-then-write is inherently racy across concurrent requests, so the handler wraps the whole attempt in a bounded retry keyed on a duplicate-key failure. [Rubric §8, Data Architecture] assesses id strategy and ownership of key space: a reserved range keeps two writers (the app and Sessionize) in one integer column without a coordination service. [Rubric §29, Resilience & Business Continuity] assesses whether transient conflicts are absorbed rather than surfaced: the retry is bounded to three attempts (AddRoomHandler.cs:25) so a genuine exhaustion or a real bug still fails fast rather than spinning. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability]: the collision path logs a warning naming the attempt number (:138-139), so the race is visible in telemetry instead of silent.
    • Walkthrough: three parts. (1) HandleAsync (AddRoomHandler.cs:28-61) is pure retry policy. An explicit command.RoomId short-circuits to a single attempt with no recomputation, because a collision on a caller-supplied id is a genuine caller error (:32-35). Otherwise it loops: attempt 1 runs against the ambient unit of work (:43-44); every later attempt opens scopeFactory.CreateAsyncScope() and resolves a fresh IUnitOfWork from it (:51-53), because the ambient DbContext still tracks the failed insert and the whole body (including the event load) must re-run against a clean context (:46-50). The catch filter is narrow, attempt < MaxManualIdAttempts && IsUniqueKeyViolation(ex) (:55), so anything else propagates. (2) AddRoomCoreAsync (:68-117) is one attempt: load the event and fail NotFound if absent (:73-76); when command.RoomId is null, take a read repository for Room and GetAllAsync every room in the reserved range with ignoreQueryFilters: true so soft-deleted rows still reserve their ids (:84-89), compute Max(r => r.Id) + 1 or the range start when empty (:91-93), and fail with Error.Failure(..., "Manual room ID range exhausted.") if that passes the range end (:95-96); then delegate to entity.AddRoom(roomId, command.Name, command.Sort, command.Capacity, command.Floor, command.Location, command.AccessibilityInfo) (:101-108), propagate domain errors (:109-110), SaveChangesAsync (:112), log LogRoomAdded (:114, :135-136), and return the mapped RoomDTO (:116). (3) IsUniqueKeyViolation (:124-133) walks the whole InnerException chain looking for the substring "duplicate key" with OrdinalIgnoreCase (:126-129).
    • Why it's built this way: the aggregate owns room creation invariants, while the handler owns the one concern no single event can decide, namely an id range that is global across all events (AddRoomHandler.cs:78-80). Detection is message-based rather than typed on a SQL exception because the Application layer is not allowed to reference EF Core or provider types (:119-123), which is Clean Architecture's dependency rule paying a small cost in precision; the comment records that both SQL Server errors 2601 and 2627 report "duplicate key". Retrying in a new scope instead of reusing the failed one is the load-bearing detail: reusing the attempt's already-mutated Event would append a second room and re-raise its domain event, and attaching that instance to another context is not permitted (:46-50).
    • Where it's used: dispatched by the rooms controller through the CQRS pipeline for AddRoomCommand (MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/RoomsController.cs:150).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the retry treats every attempt after the first as scope-fresh, so an attempt that fails for a non-duplicate reason is not retried at all (the filter excludes it) and surfaces as a thrown exception to the pipeline's exception middleware. IsUniqueKeyViolation matches on message text, so a provider that words its duplicate-key error differently would not be recognized; that risk is acknowledged in the comment (AddRoomHandler.cs:119-123) but not guarded in source.

    EventDTOMapper

    MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application.Events.DTOs · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application/Events/DTOs/EventDTOMapper.cs:14 · Level 9 · class (sealed partial)

    • What it is: the mapper from an Event aggregate to an EventDTO. Unlike the three flat mappers in this unit it composes the child mappers for rooms, speakers, and answers, and it hand-patches the one property Mapperly cannot generate.
    • Depends on: IEntityDTOMapper<TEntity, TEntityDTO, TIdentifierType> (EventDTOMapper.cs:3,18), the three child mappers RoomDTOMapper, EventSpeakerDTOMapper, and EventQuestionAnswerDTOMapper (EventDTOMapper.cs:15-17), Event and EventDTO (EventDTOMapper.cs:1-2), Mapperly (NuGet, EventDTOMapper.cs:4), and System.Globalization.CultureInfo (EventDTOMapper.cs:39).
    • Concept introduced, [UseMapper] composition plus a post-generation patch. Two Mapperly techniques appear here that the flat mappers do not need. First, [UseMapper] on a field tells the generator "when you need to map this child type, call that mapper", so a parent map reuses the child maps instead of re-declaring them (EventDTOMapper.cs:20-27). Second, when one property needs a conversion the generator cannot express, the pattern is not to abandon generation: the public method is hand-written, it calls a private generated map, and it patches the one property afterwards with a with expression. The private generated map is told to skip that property via [MapperIgnoreTarget] (EventDTOMapper.cs:50-51), so the generator does not emit a competing (and failing) conversion. [Rubric §1, SOLID] assesses composition over duplication: the room map is defined once in RoomDTOMapper and reused here. [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality]: the hand-written escape hatch is one property wide and adjacent to a comment naming exactly why it exists (EventDTOMapper.cs:35), rather than a full hand-rolled map.
    • Walkthrough: the primary constructor takes the three child mappers (EventDTOMapper.cs:14-17) and stores each in a [UseMapper]-attributed readonly field (:20-27). The public MapToDTO (:30-41) null-guards the entity (:32), calls the private generated MapToDTOGenerated(entity) (:33), then returns dto with { LastSessionizeRefreshBy = entity.LastSessionizeRefreshBy?.ToString(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture) } (:36-40): the entity holds a nullable UserIdentifierType while the DTO exposes a nullable string, a conversion the comment records as not expressible in Mapperly (:35). MapToDTOs (:44-48) is the standard null-guarded batch over the public MapToDTO, so every element gets the patch too. The generated map itself is the private partial EventDTO MapToDTOGenerated(Event entity) carrying [MapperIgnoreTarget(nameof(EventDTO.LastSessionizeRefreshBy))] (:50-51).
    • Why it's built this way: routing the batch through the public MapToDTO rather than the generated one is what keeps the patch from being silently skipped on list endpoints, which is the failure mode this shape avoids. Delegating child collections to [UseMapper] keeps each child map in one file and means a change to RoomDTO is picked up by the event map with no edit here. Using CultureInfo.InvariantCulture on the ToString keeps the wire value stable regardless of server locale, which the analyzers enforce anyway.
    • Where it's used: injected into CreateEventHandler (Events/UseCases/Create/CreateEventHandler.cs:19) and UpdateEventHandler (Events/UseCases/Update/UpdateEventHandler.cs:18), and resolved for the event read paths through the generic query service. Registered by Scrutor assembly scanning (MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application/DependencyInjection.cs:106).
    • Caveats / not-in-source: the DTO exposes the last Sessionize refresh actor as a stringified identifier, not a display name; no lookup to Identity happens here, so consumers get the raw id text.

    EventCreateRequest

    MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application.Events.UseCases.Create · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application/Events/UseCases/Create/EventCreateRequest.cs:10 · Level 8 · record

    • What it is: the inbound contract for creating a conference Event. It is both the HTTP request body and the command that the CQRS pipeline dispatches: there is no separate CreateEventCommand.

    • Concept introduced, the create request as the command. Every other write in this unit has a hand-written XxxCommand record. Create does not: implementing the marker ICreateRequest (EventCreateRequest.cs:10) is what lets the generic create machinery in Group 12 accept this record straight off the wire, hand it to an IEntityRequestMapper, and dispatch it as ICommandHandler<EventCreateRequest, Result<EventDTO>>. One record therefore carries three roles: the JSON contract, the validation target, and the command. required on Name, StartDate, EndDate, and TimeZone (EventCreateRequest.cs:19,25,28,31) makes the mandatory set a compile-time property of the type rather than a convention the deserializer has to be trusted with, and every member is init-only so the request cannot be mutated after model binding. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses whether inbound contracts are explicit about shape and optionality: the split between four required members and six nullable ones is the API's optionality documentation. [Rubric §5, Vertical Slice] assesses whether a feature's request, validator, mapper, and handler live together: all four Create types sit in one folder.

Id (EventCreateRequest.cs:16) is a non-nullable EventIdentifierType, so an omitted id binds to 0; the domain factory discards whatever arrives when Event's key is store-generated (MMCA.ADC.Conference.Domain/Events/Event.cs:151,164). Then the four required fields, Name, StartDate, EndDate, TimeZone (EventCreateRequest.cs:19,25,28,31), where TimeZone is an IANA identifier rather than a UTC offset, and finally the optional Description, SessionizeCode, VenueAddress, VenueMapUrl, WiFiInfo (EventCreateRequest.cs:22,34,37,40,43). SessionizeCode is the hook that later lets RefreshFromSessionizeCommand pull an agenda for this event.
    • Why it's built this way: collapsing request and command removes a mapping step that would have no behavior of its own, while the marker interfaces keep caching and pipeline participation declarative instead of hand-coded in the handler. Storing an IANA zone id rather than a fixed offset is what lets session times render correctly across a daylight-saving boundary.
    • Where it's used: bound by the events controller (MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/EventsController.cs:233) and injected there as ICommandHandler<EventCreateRequest, Result<EventDTO>> (EventsController.cs:46); validated by EventCreateRequestValidator, converted by EventCreateRequestMapper, handled by CreateEventHandler. Its edit-side counterpart is EventUpdateRequest.

    PublishEventCommand

    MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application.Events.UseCases.Publish · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application/Events/UseCases/Publish/PublishEventCommand.cs:12 · Level 8 · record (sealed)

    • What it is: the write intent for flipping an Event to published, which is what makes it visible to attendees. It carries the event id and, optionally, the concurrency token the client last saw.
    • Depends on: ICacheInvalidating (PublishEventCommand.cs:2,12), the Event type for the cache prefix (PublishEventCommand.cs:1,15), and the EventIdentifierType alias.
    • Concept introduced, the optional optimistic-concurrency token on a state-transition command. byte[]? RowVersion = null (PublishEventCommand.cs:12) is a defaulted positional parameter, so the command compiles and dispatches with or without it. When present it is the SQL Server rowversion the client received on its last read; the handler stamps it back as the row's original value so the UPDATE matches zero rows if anyone else changed the event in the meantime, and the save surfaces a 409 Conflict. When it is null the check is skipped entirely. Making it opt-in rather than mandatory is the deliberate choice recorded in ADR-035: a state transition is the classic lost-update target (two organizers looking at the same stale draft), but internal callers such as the Sessionize import do not need to carry a token. [Rubric §8, Data Architecture] assesses how concurrent writes are reconciled: the token turns a silent last-writer-wins into an explicit conflict the caller must resolve. [Rubric §9, API & Contract Design] assesses contract explicitness: the token is part of the command, not an ambient header the handler has to go looking for.
    • Walkthrough: two positional parameters, EventIdentifierType Id and byte[]? RowVersion (PublishEventCommand.cs:12), plus the computed CachePrefix => $"{typeof(Event).FullName}:" (PublishEventCommand.cs:15). There is no validation and no behavior on the record; the "already published" rule lives on the aggregate (MMCA.ADC.Conference.Domain/Events/Event.cs:226-233).
    • Why it's built this way: publishing is a domain transition, not a field edit, so it gets its own command rather than riding on the update request. That keeps the authorization surface, the audit log line, and the cache eviction distinct from a generic edit, and it lets the API expose a purpose-named endpoint instead of a PATCH of a boolean.
    • Where it's used: constructed by the events controller from the route id plus the request body's token (MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/EventsController.cs:279, handler injected at :48) and handled by PublishEventHandler. Its inverse is UnpublishEventCommand.

    MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application.Events.UseCases.RemoveEventQuestionAnswer · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application/Events/UseCases/RemoveEventQuestionAnswer/RemoveEventQuestionAnswerCommand.cs:9 · Level 8 · record (sealed)

An add carries the child's payload and an optional child id; a remove carries only the aggregate id plus the child id, because the child already exists and the only decision left is which one. The pair (EventId, EventQuestionAnswerId) is what makes the operation aggregate-scoped: the handler loads the event and asks it to remove the answer, so a caller cannot delete an answer by id alone and bypass the aggregate's rules. The cache prefix is again keyed on Event, not on the child, because a cached event read carries its answers inline. RemoveEventSpeakerCommand and RemoveRoomCommand are the same two-identifier record with a different child. [Rubric §4, Domain-Driven Design] assesses whether children are mutated through their root: the command's shape makes any other access path impossible to express. [Rubric §10, Cross-Cutting]: cache eviction attaches by marker interface, so no removal handler contains cache code.

Notably there is no owner id and no RowVersion: ownership is derived server-side from the ambient user by RemoveEventQuestionAnswerHandler, and there is no accompanying validator class in the folder because two required identifiers have nothing to check beyond model binding.
    • Why it's built this way: keeping the payload to two identifiers means the ownership rule (BR-52/BR-53) cannot be spoofed by the caller; the handler reads the answer's CreatedBy from the database instead of trusting the request.

    MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application.Events.UseCases.Create · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application/Events/UseCases/Create/EventCreateRequestMapper.cs:11 · Level 9 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the one adapter that turns an EventCreateRequest into an Event domain entity, by calling the aggregate's Create factory and returning whatever Result it produces.
    • Depends on: IEntityRequestMapper<TEntity, TCreateRequest, TIdentifierType> from MMCA.Common.Application.Interfaces (EventCreateRequestMapper.cs:2,11-12), the Event aggregate and its EventIdentifierType alias (EventCreateRequestMapper.cs:1), and Result<T> from MMCA.Common.Shared.Abstractions (EventCreateRequestMapper.cs:3,15).
    • Concept introduced, request-to-entity mapping as a separate injectable role. The generic create pipeline never constructs entities itself; it resolves an IEntityRequestMapper<TEntity, TCreateRequest, TIdentifierType> and asks it for one. That indirection is what lets one handler shape serve every aggregate while each aggregate keeps its own construction rules. Two properties of this mapper matter. First, it is a plain sealed class with no [Mapper] attribute (EventCreateRequestMapper.cs:11): unlike the read-side DTO mappers, request-to-entity conversion is deliberately hand-written, because it must go through a factory that can fail, which a property-copy generator cannot express. Second, it returns Task<Result<Event>> rather than an Event, so an invalid request produces a failure value that flows back through the handler as a 400-class response instead of an exception. [Rubric §3, Clean Architecture] assesses whether the domain stays independent of the delivery mechanism: the controller knows a request type, the domain knows a factory, and this class is the only thing that knows both. [Rubric §4, Domain-Driven Design]: the factory stays the single construction path, so no invariant can be bypassed by new. See ADR-001 for the no-reflection mapping policy.
    • Walkthrough: one method. CreateEntityAsync(EventCreateRequest request, CancellationToken) (EventCreateRequestMapper.cs:15) null-guards with ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(request) (EventCreateRequestMapper.cs:17), then returns Task.FromResult(Event.Create(...)) forwarding all ten request fields positionally, Id, Name, Description, StartDate, EndDate, TimeZone, SessionizeCode, VenueAddress, VenueMapUrl, WiFiInfo (EventCreateRequestMapper.cs:19-29). The factory's eleventh parameter, questionModerationDefault, is not forwarded and takes its declared default of QuestionModerationDefault.Pending (MMCA.ADC.Conference.Domain/Events/Event.cs:142), so a newly created event starts with moderated questions. The method is synchronous in substance: Task.FromResult satisfies the async contract without allocating a state machine, because the factory does no I/O. The forwarded Id is discarded by the factory when the aggregate's key is store-generated (Event.cs:151,164).
    • Why it's built this way: pushing construction into Event.Create means invariant checks (EventInvariants.EnsureNameIsValid, EnsureTimeZoneIsValid, EnsureDateRangeIsValid, combined at Event.cs:144-147) run even for callers that never touch the HTTP layer, such as the Sessionize import. The mapper adds no rules of its own, which is exactly what makes it safe to have several entry points.
    • Where it's used: injected into CreateEventHandler as IEntityRequestMapper<Event, EventCreateRequest, EventIdentifierType> (CreateEventHandler.cs:18), registered by the module's assembly scanning rather than an explicit AddScoped line (MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application/DependencyInjection.cs).

    EventCreateRequestValidator

    MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application.Events.UseCases.Create · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application/Events/UseCases/Create/EventCreateRequestValidator.cs:7 · Level 9 · class (sealed)

    • What it is: the FluentValidation validator the pipeline runs against an EventCreateRequest before CreateEventHandler sees it. It contains no rules of its own: it is three Include calls.
    • Depends on: FluentValidation.AbstractValidator<T> (NuGet, EventCreateRequestValidator.cs:1,7) and the three shared rule objects EventNameRules<T>, EventTimeZoneRules<T>, and EventDateRangeRules<T> from MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application.Events.Validation (EventCreateRequestValidator.cs:2,11-13).
    • Concept introduced, rule composition by Include with a property selector. FluentValidation's Include(otherValidator) copies every rule from another AbstractValidator<T> into this one, and it requires both validators to be generic over the same T. That is why the rule classes are generic in the containing type and take an expression selector in their constructor: new EventNameRules<EventCreateRequest>(p => p.Name) (EventCreateRequestValidator.cs:11) says "apply the event-name rules to this type's Name property". The same three rule classes are re-included by EventUpdateRequestValidator against a different request type, so a length or format constraint is written once and both slices inherit it: there is no way for create and update to drift apart on what a valid event name is. Note also which rules exist and which do not: name, time zone, and the start-before-end date range are validated, while the optional URL and venue fields are not constrained here. [Rubric §24, Forms, Validation & UX Safety] assesses whether invalid input is rejected at the boundary with actionable messages: the request never reaches the aggregate when a rule fails. [Rubric §16, Maintainability]: a shared rule object is one edit point instead of N. [Rubric §1, SOLID]: each rule class has one reason to change, and validators compose them rather than inherit a fat base.
    • Walkthrough: the whole type is a constructor. EventCreateRequestValidator() (EventCreateRequestValidator.cs:9-14) calls Include(new EventNameRules<EventCreateRequest>(p => p.Name)) (:11), Include(new EventTimeZoneRules<EventCreateRequest>(p => p.TimeZone)) (:12), and Include(new EventDateRangeRules<EventCreateRequest>(p => p.StartDate, p => p.EndDate)) (:13). The date-range rule takes two selectors because it is a cross-field rule, which is the reason it cannot be expressed as a per-property attribute. The rule bodies live in MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application/Events/Validation/EventValidationRules.cs:13,25,55 and delegate to the same EventInvariants constants the domain factory uses.
    • Why it's built this way: validating at the pipeline boundary gives the caller a complete, field-addressed error list in one round trip, while the domain factory keeps its own invariant checks as the backstop for non-HTTP callers. The duplication is intentional and cheap because both sides read the same EventInvariants limits.
    • Where it's used: resolved by the validation decorator around CreateEventHandler; the update-side sibling is EventUpdateRequestValidator.

    PublishEventHandler

    MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application.Events.UseCases.Publish · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application/Events/UseCases/Publish/PublishEventHandler.cs:13 · Level 9 · class (sealed partial)

    • What it is: the handler for PublishEventCommand. It loads the event, stamps the client's concurrency token, asks the aggregate to publish itself, and saves only if the aggregate agreed.
    • Depends on: IUnitOfWork (PublishEventHandler.cs:3,14), ILogger<T> with a source-generated [LoggerMessage] (PublishEventHandler.cs:1,15,41-42), ICommandHandler<in TCommand, TResult> (PublishEventHandler.cs:4,15), the Event aggregate (PublishEventHandler.cs:2), and Result / Error (PublishEventHandler.cs:5).
    • Concept introduced, applying an optimistic-concurrency token to a loaded entity. The interesting line is repository.SetOriginalRowVersion(entity, command.RowVersion) (PublishEventHandler.cs:29). EF Core decides whether an UPDATE succeeded by comparing the row's original tracked rowversion against the database. Normally the original value is whatever the row had when it was just loaded, which is by definition current, so a concurrency check would always pass. This call overwrites the tracked original with the token the client last saw (IRepository<TEntity, TIdentifierType> declares it at MMCA.Common.Application/Interfaces/Infrastructure/IRepository.cs:173), so a decision made against a stale view fails the save and surfaces as 409 Conflict rather than silently overwriting a concurrent edit. Passing null is the documented way to skip the check (PublishEventHandler.cs:27-29). This is ADR-035 in three lines. [Rubric §8, Data Architecture] assesses concurrency and consistency handling: the check is in the database, not in an application-side read-then-compare that could itself race. [Rubric §13, Observability & Operability]: the source-generated log message means the transition is recorded with structured fields at zero allocation when the level is disabled.
    • Walkthrough: primary-constructor injection of IUnitOfWork and ILogger<PublishEventHandler> (PublishEventHandler.cs:13-15), and the class implements ICommandHandler<PublishEventCommand, Result>. HandleAsync (PublishEventHandler.cs:18-39) gets the typed repository from the unit of work (:22), loads by id with the default no-tracking-free read (:23), and returns Error.NotFound.WithSource(nameof(PublishEventHandler)).WithTarget(nameof(Event)) when the row is absent (:24-25). Note there is no includes array and no asTracking: true here: a publish touches a scalar on the root only, unlike the child-removal handlers below. It then stamps the row version (:29), calls entity.Publish() (:31), and only on success awaits unitOfWork.SaveChangesAsync(cancellationToken) and logs LogEventPublished (:32-36). The aggregate's own Result is returned unchanged (:38), so an "already published" invariant failure (MMCA.ADC.Conference.Domain/Events/Event.cs:228-232) reaches the caller with its domain error code intact. LogEventPublished is declared partial with [LoggerMessage(Level = LogLevel.Information, ...)] (:41-42) and its body is generated at build time.
    • Why it's built this way: the save-only-on-success shape is the module's canonical command body. It means a rejected transition writes nothing at all, so the single SaveChangesAsync stays the one boundary that stamps audit fields, captures domain events, and writes the outbox row for EventChanged raised inside Event.Publish (Event.cs:237).
    • Where it's used: resolved by the events controller as ICommandHandler<PublishEventCommand, Result> (MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/EventsController.cs:48) and invoked at :279. Its inverse is UnpublishEventHandler.

    RemoveEventQuestionAnswerHandler

    MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application.Events.UseCases.RemoveEventQuestionAnswer · MMCA.ADC.Conference.Application/Events/UseCases/RemoveEventQuestionAnswer/RemoveEventQuestionAnswerHandler.cs:14 · Level 9 · class (sealed partial)

    • What it is: the handler for RemoveEventQuestionAnswerCommand. Beyond the usual load-mutate-save shape it enforces BR-52/BR-53: an Attendee may delete only their own answer, an Organizer may delete any.
    • Depends on: IUnitOfWork (RemoveEventQuestionAnswerHandler.cs:3,15), ICurrentUserService (RemoveEventQuestionAnswerHandler.cs:6,16), ILogger<T> (:17,54-55), the Event aggregate and its EventQuestionAnswer child (:2), RoleNames (:6,35), and Result / Error (:5).
    • Concept introduced, row-level ownership authorization inside the handler. Role-based authorization on the controller can answer "may this caller call this endpoint"; it cannot answer "may this caller touch this row". That second question needs the row, so it is asked here, after the aggregate is loaded and before the mutation. The check has three moving parts (RemoveEventQuestionAnswerHandler.cs:34-42): find the non-deleted answer by id in the loaded collection, ask ICurrentUserService whether the caller holds the Organizer role, and compare the answer's audit field CreatedBy with the caller's UserId. The identity is read from the ambient authenticated principal, never from the command, which is why RemoveEventQuestionAnswerCommand has no owner field to spoof. Failure returns Error.Forbidden(code: "EventQuestionAnswer.NotOwner", ...) (:37-41), a distinct error kind that the API layer maps to 403 rather than 404. [Rubric §11, Security] assesses whether authorization is enforced where the data is, not only at the edge: the ownership decision is made against the persisted CreatedBy, so a forged request cannot win it. [Rubric §10, Cross-Cutting]: the ambient user arrives through one injected abstraction, so the same rule reads identically in the update sibling.
    • Walkthrough: primary-constructor injection of the unit of work, the current-user service, and the logger (RemoveEventQuestionAnswerHandler.cs:14-17). HandleAsync (:20-52) loads the event with its answers and with tracking on, includes: [nameof(Event.EventQuestionAnswers)], asTracking: true (:25-29), which is required because the removal walks the child collection and EF must be tracking it for the change to be persisted. Missing event yields Error.NotFound (:30-31). The ownership check follows (:34-42); note it is written defensively as answer is not null && ..., so a request naming an answer that does not exist falls through to the domain method rather than returning 403, and the domain reports the not-found condition. entity.RemoveEventQuestionAnswer(command.EventQuestionAnswerId) (:44) performs the soft delete inside the aggregate, and only on success does the handler save and log (:45-49). The result of the domain call is returned as-is (:51).
    • Why it's built this way: keeping the ownership rule in the handler rather than in the aggregate keeps Event free of any notion of "who is calling", which is an application concern, while keeping it out of the controller means every caller of this command gets the rule, including future non-HTTP entry points.
    • Where it's used: resolved by the answers controller as ICommandHandler<RemoveEventQuestionAnswerCommand, Result> (MMCA.ADC.Conference.API/Controllers/EventQuestionAnswersController.cs:60) and invoked at :194. Its update sibling is UpdateEventQuestionAnswerHandler; its add counterpart is AddEventQuestionAnswerHandler.

The handler itself contributes only sequencing and a log line, and there is no new Event(...) anywhere in it. Note also what is absent: no validator call (the pipeline's validation decorator already ran EventCreateRequestValidator), no cache eviction (the caching decorator reads CachePrefix off EventCreateRequest), and no try/catch (failures arrive as Result values). That absence is the point of the decorator pipeline taught in Group 05. [Rubric §5, Vertical Slice] assesses whether a use case is self-contained: the four Create types live in one folder and this handler is the slice's entry point. [Rubric §3, Clean Architecture]: the Application layer depends on abstractions (IUnitOfWork, IEntityRequestMapper) and on the Domain, never on EF Core or ASP.NET. [Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven]: one command type, one handler, one write path, and the EventChanged domain event raised inside the factory (MMCA.ADC.Conference.Domain/Events/Event.cs:168) is captured by the same SaveChangesAsync.

It then unwraps result.Value! (:31), gets unitOfWork.GetRepository<Event, EventIdentifierType>() (:32), awaits repository.AddAsync(entity, cancellationToken) and then the single unitOfWork.SaveChangesAsync(cancellationToken) (:34-35), both with .ConfigureAwait(false). After the save it emits the generated LogEventCreated(logger, entity.Id, entity.Name) (:37, declaration :42-43), which is placed after the save so the logged id is the store-generated key rather than a placeholder. It returns Result.Success(dtoMapper.MapToDTO(entity)) (:39).

Id (:16) is present for contract symmetry but its XML comment states plainly that the handler auto-generates it and caller-provided values are ignored. QuestionText (:19) is the one required member. QuestionEntity (:22) and QuestionType (:25) are nullable strings that the domain later constrains to a fixed vocabulary. Sort (:28) drives display order and IsRequired (:31) marks the question mandatory.
    • Why it's built this way: init-only members plus required on the one non-negotiable field give compile-time enforcement of the minimum payload while leaving the rest optional, and collapsing request and command into one type keeps a simple create slice to a single message (contrast the child-add flows, where the controller builds a distinct command record).
    • Where it's used: bound by QuestionsController (Group 20); validated by QuestionCreateRequestValidator; translated to a domain entity by QuestionCreateRequestMapper; handled by CreateQuestionHandler.
    • Caveats / not-in-source: Id is a settable part of the public contract even though it is always overwritten. The override is visible in the handler (CreateQuestionHandler.cs:87), not on this type, so reading the record alone would suggest the caller controls the id.

[Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability] and [Rubric §15, Best Practices & Code Quality] also apply: Mapperly emits the field-copy code at build time, so there is no runtime reflection, the mapping is steppable in a debugger, and an unmapped member is a build-time diagnostic instead of a silently dropped field. This is the shape every leaf mapper in the Conference module repeats.

The single-entity method is declared but not written: public partial QuestionDTO MapToDTO(Question entity) (:16), and the generator supplies the body. The collection overload MapToDTOs (:19-23) is hand-written: it null-guards with ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull (:21) and projects with a collection expression over the generated single-entity method ([.. entityCollection.Select(MapToDTO)], :22).

    • Where it's used: injected into CreateQuestionHandler (CreateQuestionHandler.cs:23) to project the created entity, and resolved by the question read path for list and detail responses.

Same contract as AddSpeakerCategoryItemCommand, but the prefix is the parent aggregate's: CachePrefix => $"{typeof(Event).FullName}:" (UpdateRoomCommand.cs:26). That is the interesting detail. Rooms have no independent cache namespace, so editing a room invalidates the whole Event cache surface, which is what keeps a stale nested room out of an already-cached event read. [Rubric §6, CQRS & Event-Driven], [Rubric §12, Performance & Scalability].
    • Walkthrough: a sealed record with eight positional parameters (UpdateRoomCommand.cs:15-23): EventId and RoomId locate the child; Name (:18) and Sort (:19) are required scalars; Capacity (:20), Floor (:21), Location (:22), and AccessibilityInfo (:23) are the optional organizer-entered details. The parameter list is exactly the argument list of Event.UpdateRoom (MMCA.ADC.Conference.Domain/Events/Event.cs:368-375), so the handler forwards without reshaping.

[Rubric §24, Forms, Validation & UX Safety] assesses whether input is checked before business logic executes and whether the message returned is usable by a UI. The class is sealed with an expression-bodied constructor holding one rule (AddSpeakerCategoryItemCommandValidator.cs:10-13): RuleFor(x => x.CategoryItemId).NotEqual(default(CategoryItemIdentifierType)).WithMessage("Category item ID is required."). It is discovered by the module's assembly scan and run by ValidatingCommandDecorator<TCommand, TResult>, which sits ahead of the transactional decorator, so a malformed command never opens a database transaction.

The deeper rule (is this category item already attached to the speaker?) needs the loaded aggregate and therefore lives in Speaker.AddSpeakerCategoryItem, which returns the Speaker.CategoryItem.Duplicate invariant error (MMCA.ADC.Conference.Domain/Speakers/Speaker.cs:299-305). Splitting "is the request well-formed?" from "is the operation allowed?" keeps each concern in one place, and a new command is wired simply by the existence of a validator class.
